meeting_header:
Date: 2025-11-18 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 47m
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Sofia Ramos (CTO, Veridian), Ethan Park (Backend Lead), Maya Singh (ML Engineer), Carlos Jimenez (SRE)
summary: POC scoping focused on integrating Veridian's inference scripts with Redwood's benchmark harness. Key topics: streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs, script adapters, concurrency targets, token distributions, KV cache impacts, auth/VPC setup. Agreed next steps and owners for harness template, sample scripts, and staging run schedule.
transcript:
[00:00:00] Ava (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick roll call and then we'll dive into the harness details.
[00:00:12] Sofia (Veridian): Hi — Sofia here. We have Ethan, Maya and Carlos on. Thanks.
[00:00:20] Ava: Great. Goal for today: capture the workloads, define the success criteria for the POC, and agree on what scripts you can provide vs what Redwood will adapt. Also pick streaming vs non-streaming tests.
[00:00:35] Ethan: Quick context — our primary product is a clinical notes summarization API. Typical request sizes are 600-1,200 tokens, but we also have some long-form reports up to ~7k tokens. Latency target is 300-700ms P95 for short prompts, and we care about cost per 1k tokens.
[00:00:55] Liam (Redwood): Thanks. For the harness we'll need both the short-path and long-path templates. Do you have p95 distributions by endpoint?
[00:01:05] Maya: We have histograms but they're messy. I can pull average and 95th percentiles — most calls are 900 tokens median.
[00:01:12] Priya (Redwood): Also helpful: do you stream to clients today or return full responses?
[00:01:18] Ethan: We stream on the websocket channel for interactive flows, but batch returns are used in async pipelines.
[00:01:25] Ava: Perfect: that means we should test both streaming (open connection, partial tokens) and non-streaming (full response). The harness supports both modes; the adapter pattern is to wrap your tokenizer + request builder.
[00:01:38] Carlos: Quick Q on KV cash — I mean KV cache — how much does that impact throughput for repeated prefixes?
[00:01:43] Liam: Good question. For autoregressive models, KV caching reduces compute per token on repeated context by about 20–60% depending on sequence length and model. We'll capture that in the benchmark as separate test legs: cold start, warm cache, and sustained cache.
[00:01:58] Sofia: Success criteria from our side: 1) meet latency SLOs for short prompts, 2) achieve <30% cost increase vs base open-source quantized model, and 3) stable throughput for 48h stress run.
[00:02:12] Ava: Noted. We'll translate that into quantifiable test thresholds: P95 latency <= 700ms for <=1k tokens, cost per 1k tokens delta measured vs baseline run, and no more than 5% error rate over 48h.
[00:02:25] Maya: On accuracy — we need regression checks vs our golden prompt set. Can the harness run round-trip evals?
[00:02:30] Liam: Yes, we can plug in your eval scripts. We typically run n=500 golden prompts during benchmark runs and compute similarity/regression metrics. Send us the set and the pass/fail thresholds you care about.
[00:02:42] Ethan: For concurrency targets, what does Redwood recommend as a starting point? We're thinking 2k concurrent users for production peak (mostly short prompts).
[00:02:50] Priya: For a POC, we like to scale in steps: 50, 200, 500, 1k, 2k. We'll define a load profile that progressively increases RPS and keeps track of latencies and token throughput.
[00:03:02] Carlos: About auth — we'll be using our internal token service and prefer not to hand over long-lived creds. Can we use short-lived tokens or a signed URL flow?
[00:03:10] Ava: Absolutely. We support ephemeral API keys and can integrate with your token service via a short-lived bearer token. For VPC/private deployments we'll do peering — for hosted POC staging we can use a secure ingress and pre-shared ephemeral tokens.
[00:03:24] Sofia: On networking, our security team will need flow logs and audit logs. Does Redwood provide request-level logs with PII redaction?
[00:03:31] Liam: Yes, we have audit logs and configurable retention. We also have a PII-redaction option in the harness that hashes or strips fields before logging. We'll share the SOC2 checklist docs.
[00:03:42] Ethan: Back to streaming vs non-streaming — what's the main cost delta?
[00:03:46] Liam: Streaming itself isn't more expensive compute-wise, but higher concurrency with many open connections can increase memory and concurrency overhead on the runtime. Non-streaming can batch more effectively which reduces per-token cost. We'll quantify this in the matrix: same total tokens served, compare latency and cost under streaming and batched non-streaming patterns.
[00:04:05] Maya: For long documents (7k tokens), what's the recommended approach in the harness? Chunking + rolling KV or full long-seq runs?
[00:04:12] Priya: We support both. For accuracy-sensitive tasks we do long-seq runs; for throughput tests we simulate chunked pipelines with context stitching and KV reuse. We'll include both in the test plan.
[00:04:24] Sofia: Timeline question — what's realistic to get an end-to-end POC with benchmark numbers?
[00:04:29] Ava: Typical POCs run 4–8 weeks. Given you have scripts and a clear golden-set, we can do initial harness setup and staging runs in 1–2 weeks, then iterative optimization and a final 48h stress run in week 3–4.
[00:04:41] Ethan: That aligns. We aim to decide by end of December.
[00:04:45] Carlos: Any limitations we should know for the staging environment? Max concurrency, rate limits, token caps?
[00:04:50] Liam: Staging can support up to modest concurrency by default but we'll provision a dedicated pool for the POC. We'll propose a dedicated 4-GPU pool for the large model leg and autoscale rules for small-model/batch legs. We'll document the exact limits in the runbook.
[00:05:06] Maya: About the harness adapter — what's the expected shape of the customer script? Do you want a container, a python function, or a series of curl examples?
[00:05:13] Priya: We accept a few forms. Most customers provide a small python harness with a tokenization wrapper and a request function. We have an adapter shim that takes that function and wires it into our runner. If you prefer containers, we can run the containerized adapter too.
[00:05:25] Ethan: We'll probably attach our internal request builder — it's a node microservice. Can Redwood run a node adapter?
[00:05:30] Liam: Yes — we have node and python adapters. The important pieces: a project that exposes a standard call signature (input prompt -> request -> parse response) and a way to report latency/tokens consumed.
[00:05:42] Carlos: On telemetry: do you capture per-token latency or only per-request? We need granularity to diagnose streaming stalls.
[00:05:47] Liam: We capture both. For streaming we emit chunk-level timestamps; for non-streaming we emit request start/end and token counts. We'll send an example telemetry CSV schema.
[00:05:57] Sofia: If we run quantized models in your environment, what control do we have over quantization and kernel selection?
[00:06:04] Liam: You can specify a quantization profile; our optimize engine will recommend kernels per hardware. For the POC we'll run both default quantized and a tuned quant profile to compare quality vs latency/cost.
[00:06:17] Ava: Let's outline the success criteria concretely so we have a shared target: (1) P95 latency <= 700ms for <=1k token path under 2k concurrent simulated users; (2) cost delta <= +30% vs your baseline quantized model; (3) accuracy regression <= 3% on golden set; (4) no more than 5% error rate during 48h stress. Agreed?
[00:06:39] Sofia: Yes, that seems fair.
[00:06:41] Ethan: On measurement methodology, are you running tests with client-side timing or server-side timing?
[00:06:45] Priya: Both. We'll run client-side synthetic traffic to simulate networking and also capture server-side metrics for exact processing times. We'll correlate them in the dashboards.
[00:06:55] Maya: Any particular artifacts you need for golden set? We have samples tied to PII that we can't share.
[00:07:01] Ava: We can accept redacted or synthetic equivalents. If needed, run the harness in your VPC and we can point the runner there so the data never leaves your network.
[00:07:10] Carlos: That would be preferable for the long-form reports.
[00:07:13] Liam: On the practical side for integration: pls zip up a minimal adapter example — tokenization snippet, request builder, and a small test set (10 prompts) for initial smoke. We'll run the smoke and then the scaled runs.
[00:07:26] Ethan: OK we'll provide that.
[00:07:28] Ava: About reporting: we'll produce a benchmark report that contains throughput, latency percentiles, token metrics, cost model, kernel/quantization notes, and regression metrics vs golden set. Also we'll include suggestions (batching config, cache warms, route policies).
[00:07:42] Sofia: How do you handle intermittent model fallbacks? If the dedicated pool is saturated, will requests fail or fallback to a cheaper model?
[00:07:49] Liam: By default we recommend a graceful fallback policy: route to compatible model variant when latency or capacity thresholds exceed. During the POC we can test fallback behavior as a separate shock test.
[00:07:59] Priya: We'll add a canary and automatic fallback leg to the test matrix.
[00:08:03] Maya: Anything about A/B testing during the POC? We want to compare quantized vs full-fp on accuracy.
[00:08:08] Ava: Yes, we can run A/B sampling and feed the results into the eval pipeline. We'll make sure the harness marks each sample's variant for regression calculation.
[00:08:17] Ethan: One more on monitoring: do you expose Prometheus metrics? We want to plug into our dashboards.
[00:08:21] Liam: Yep — Prometheus endpoints and Grafana dashboards. We'll share a dashboard JSON you can import.
[00:08:27] Carlos: Ok, let's recap next steps.
[00:08:30] Ava: Recap: Redwood sends harness template and example node adapter; customer provides tokenized sample prompts, minimal adapter, and network info; schedule access setup call; run smoke then staged scale ups.
[00:08:42] Sofia: Sounds good.
[00:08:44] Ethan: Two logistic details — estimated credits/costs for POC?
[00:08:49] Ava: We'll send a provisional POC pricing sheet. Usually we include a small cloud credit allowance and list expected GPU hours per test leg.
[00:08:58] Maya: Any gotchas you've seen in similar customers?
[00:09:02] Liam: The common ones: tokenization mismatch (off-by-one in tokenizer), hidden client-side batching, and under-specified retry behavior causing replay storms. We'll include checklist items to validate those.
[00:09:15] Priya: Also watch for header mismatch when streaming — some client libs buffer until connection close. We'll include a streaming test harness note.
[00:09:24] Sofia: Great — thank you.
[00:09:26] Ava: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the links and schedule.
[00:09:30] [END RECORDING]

Notes on transcription: Some words may be slightly off (KV cash -> KV cache, shammel -> SAML), filler words and short crosstalk preserved.
